To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the spatial structure of Middle Earth can be represented in language, and that people can derive spatial representations from language, maps, and a combination of both.

the spatial structure of Middle Earth was represented by the co-occurrences in Tolkien's texts of city names, that this spatial structure was encoded in the language, and that the language-based spatial structure could be used to derive a mental map of the cities in Middle Earth.

(i) the spatial locations of cities are encoded in the language of Tolkien's texts, (ii) the spatial locations encoded in language are used by humans to form cognitive maps, (iii) human spatial estimates of cities' location are very similar regardless of the information source (text or maps), and (iv) human estimates of the spatial location of cities from language are better explained by the linguistic frequencies of the cities than by the map-based locations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how we represent the spatial structure of the environment in our mind, and how we can learn to represent spatial structure through language and maps.
spatial cognition and how people mentally represent spatial information.
the representation of spatial information in the mind, how it is encoded in language and how it is represented in memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
language can encode the spatial structure of cities and that human spatial estimates can be formed from linguistic and nonlinguistic information.
language encodes the spatial structure of cities.
language and maps both encode spatial structure and that human spatial representations can come from language, from maps, or from a combination of both.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spatial structure of Middle Earth is represented in both maps and language.
spatial mental representations can be formed from statistical patterns of language.
the spatial structure of cities in Middle Earth can be represented through linguistic frequencies, maps, and human spatial estimates, and that these three representations can predict one another.
The main takeaway from our work is that
language can be used as an implicit source of information about spatial structure.
spatial structure can be represented through language, and that language can be used to represent spatial structure.
spatial mental representations can be formed from linguistic sources of information. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2022 APA, all rights reserved)
